You Already Know How to Count in Japanese 🧵

Hokage titles, Yonko, and Sannin have been teaching you Japanese numbers all along

代 (dai) means "generation" or "era of succession." 目 (me) is an ordinal suffix that turns any number into "nth" - the same way -th works in English. Put them together: 代目 means "nth holder of a position" or "nth in a line of succession.

The traditional sumo ranking list above - called a banzuke (番付) - is the same culture that produces anime's numbered hierarchies. 番 (ban) means number or ranking, 付 (zuke) means attached. A ranking with numbers attached. Sound familiar?

三代目 (sandaime) means "the third-generation holder" of the Hokage title. 三 (san) = 3, 代 (dai) = generation or succession, 目 (me) = ordinal suffix. The Third Hokage, Hiruzen Sarutobi, carries this title.

三人 (sannin) literally means "three people." 三 (san) = 3, 人 (nin) = person or people counter. The legendary Sannin - Jiraiya, Tsunade, and Orochimaru - are simply the three people at the apex of Konoha's shinobi.

七代目 (nanadaime) means "the seventh-generation Hokage." 七 (nana) = 7, 代目 (daime) = nth-generation holder of a title. Naruto Uzumaki is the Nanadaime Hokage. The same counter works for any succession in Japan: company presidents, yakuza bosses, sumo champions.
十二鬼月 (Junikizuki) means "Twelve Kizuki," the twelve most powerful demons under Muzan Kibutsuji. 十二 (juni) = 12, constructed as 十 (ju, ten) + 二 (ni, two).

Bushido: The Samurai Code Running Every Anime You Watch 🧵

武士道 explained - the seven virtues behind Tanjiro's compassion, Zoro's loyalty, and Byakuya's honor

義 (Gi) is the first and most fundamental virtue. It means righteousness, justice, the right path - doing what is morally correct even when it is not convenient or profitable.

Which one surprised you most? Drop it below 👇

Giri (義理) deserves its own note. It is often translated as "duty" but it is more specific than that: it is the obligation you owe to people based on your relationships and social position. If someone helps you, you have giri to help them back.
名誉 (Meiyo) is honor, glory, reputation. This is the virtue most Westerners associate with the word "samurai" - the obsession with how one is perceived. But Bushido's concept of 名誉 is not vanity.

The Hagakure also contains this: いざという時の覚悟 (iza to iu toki no kakugo) - "resolve at the crucial moment." 覚悟 (kakugo) is a word you will hear constantly in anime: it means resolve, readiness, acceptance of consequences.
The 道 (do) character alone is worth memorizing because it transforms everything it touches. 剣道 (kendo) is not just sword sports - it is a way of living through the sword.

The Hagakure (葉隠), written by samurai Yamamoto Tsunetomo around 1716, contains the most famous quote in samurai philosophy: Bushido to wa shinu koto to mitsuketari (武士道とは死ぬことと見つけたり), meaning "The way of the samurai is found in death.

The Legend Behind Goku, Luffy and Every Anime Monkey Hero 🧵

How a 16th-century Chinese monkey conquered Japanese pop culture

Journey to the West (西遊記, Saiyūki) is one of the four great classical novels of Chinese literature.

Which one surprised you most? Drop it below 👇

What follows is a sequence where Sun Wukong refuses every limit placed on him. He acquires his magical staff - the Ruyi Jingu Bang (如意金箍棒, Nyoi Kinkkō Bō in Japanese) - from the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea.

He then crashes the gates of heaven to steal the Elixir of Immortality, learns 72 transformation techniques, masters the Somersault Cloud (筋斗雲, Kintō-un) that crosses 108,000 li in a single leap, and declares himself equal to the gods.

When you see the kanji 悟空 (Gokū) in a Dragon Ball lyric or a Saiyuki opening, you're not just reading a character's name. You're reading a Buddhist concept: 悟 (go) means enlightenment, 空 (kū) means void.
悟空 (Gokū) is a Buddhist term meaning "understanding the void" or "awakened to emptiness." 悟 (go) means to understand or be enlightened, and 空 (kū/sora) means void, sky, or emptiness.
如意棒 (Nyoibō or Nyoi-bō) means "as you wish staff" or "will-fulfilling staff." 如意 (nyoi) means "as you wish" or "at will," and 棒 (bō) means staff or rod.

Learning Japanese with Blue Bird (Naruto Shippuden Opening) 🧵

Mama, todoku, and the precise vocabulary for chasing someone who keeps getting further away

Blue Bird (青い鳥) was released in 2008 as the third opening theme for Naruto Shippuden. It was performed by Ikimono-gakari (いきものがかり, sometimes romanised as Ikimonogakari), a Japanese pop rock band formed in Kanagawa in 1999.
〜まま attaches to a verb (past た-form or negative ない-form) to express continuing in a state without change. It often carries a sense of being stuck or of inertia.
Blue Bird is 青い鳥 (aoi tori) in Japanese. Aoi (青い) means blue or blue-green - a colour word in Japanese that traditionally spans sky blue through spring green. Tori (鳥) means bird.

Blue Bird is performed by Ikimono-gakari (いきものがかり), a Japanese pop rock band from Kanagawa. The band consists of vocalist Kiyoe Yoshioka and multi-instrumentalists Yoshiki Mizuno and Hotaka Yamashita. Their name roughly translates to "The Animal Keeper.

Jiyuu no tori ni nareru (自由の鳥になれる) means "I can become a bird of freedom." Jiyuu (自由) is freedom. の connects it as a modifier: bird of freedom. Ni nareru is the potential form of ni naru (to become something) - can become, not will become.
Mama (まま) as a grammar pattern means "remaining in the state of" or "while unchanged." It attaches to a past verb form (た-form) for completed states or a negative form (ない-form) for ongoing absences.
